title: The Disappearance of Flight MH370, Part I
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant begin a two-part look at the disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370 in March 2014. They walk through the flight's departure from Kuala Lumpur, the handoff to Ho Chi Minh City air traffic control, the loss of the transponder, the Malaysian military's radar tracking of an unexplained turn, and how Inmarsat's satellite handshake pings were used to estimate arcs and the likely crash location in the southern Indian Ocean. They also discuss the Air France 447 crash as background, and the leading theory that someone on board deliberately disabled systems and the plane flew on until it ran out of fuel. Part two is teased for the crash-site search and alternative theories.
topics: Ho Chi Minh air traffic control

segments.title: Opening and ad-like promo
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with tour dates and a promo, then introduce the episode on the missing Malaysia Airlines flight MH370 and credit researcher and William Langewiesche's Atlantic article.

segments.title: Departure from Kuala Lumpur
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Boeing 777-200ER flight from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing on March 8, 2014, its passenger and crew count, the 12:42 am takeoff, the climb to 35,000 feet, and the pilots' radio calls.

segments.title: Handoff to Ho Chi Minh control and disappearance
segments.summary: The flight is handed off to Ho Chi Minh City air traffic control. Captain Zaharie's last words are 'good night Malaysian three seven zero', and the plane vanishes from radar. Ho Chi Minh City waits 18 minutes before calling Kuala Lumpur, well beyond the five-minute protocol.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Short break before the discussion of radar systems.

segments.title: Primary vs secondary radar and transponder loss
segments.summary: The hosts explain secondary radar and transponders, which send identity and altitude data, and primary radar. The transponder stopped just after the handoff, and places beyond radar coverage allow aircraft to disappear.

segments.title: Malaysian military radar tracks an unexplained turn
segments.summary: Malaysian Air Force primary radar tracked the plane for about an hour after it vanished from transponders. It turned sharply away from its planned route, crossed the Malay Peninsula, turned near Penang, and was last seen on radar near the Andaman Sea around 2 am. The military did not reveal this for a while.

segments.title: Inmarsat satellite pings and the Air France 447 background
segments.summary: Inmarsat realized its satellite data unit on the plane had been pinging satellites for hours. The hosts describe handshake logins and reboot logins, the upgrades made after Air France 447 in 2009, and the Perth ground station data.

segments.title: Arcs, BTO and BFO analysis and the leading theory
segments.summary: Burst timing offset and burst frequency offset data produced seven arcs, with the last ping around 8:19 am and a final log-on request at 9:15 am. The hosts discuss the leading theory that someone on board deliberately disabled systems, possibly depressurized the cabin, and the plane flew until fuel ran out. They recap and close, previewing part two.
